name: Panchatantra
info: The Panchatantra is an ancient Indian collection of interrelated animal fables in Sanskrit verse and prose, by an unknown author, probably composed around 300 CE and carried into Persian, Arabic and European languages.

facts.made: An unknown author, named Vishnusharma in some recensions and Vasubhaga in others, both possibly fictitious pen names; probably a Hindu, drawing on older oral and literary traditions
facts.form: Five treatises of fables in Sanskrit verse and prose inside a frame story, with a short introduction; embedded tales and epigrammatic verses; Book 1 is about 45% of the length
facts.where: No Sanskrit text before 1000 CE survives; it is read in Sanskrit recensions, in Indian and Southeast Asian versions and in translations into over 50 languages
facts.known: Animal fables with human virtues and vices; the jackals Damanaka and Karataka; the mongoose and the woman; nīti, the wise conduct of life; Kalila wa Dimna; the Fables of Bidpai; the Hebrew, Latin and English versions

t: An unknown author, named Vishnusharma in the prelude, set animal fables inside a frame story to teach three princes nīti, the wise conduct of life.
Its Middle Persian version of about 550 CE is lost, but the Arabic Kalīla wa Dimna made from it in about 750 became the source of most European versions.
Scholars disagree whether it favours unscrupulous Machiavellian politics or demands ethical conduct from those in high office.
dyk: A woman leaves her child with a pet mongoose, finds blood on its mouth and kills it, then finds the child alive and the mongoose's blood to be a snake's. The story is told in the fifth book, whose characters are almost all human.
ev: Scholarly consensus places the composition of the Panchatantra around this year, which Patrick Olivelle calls only an educated guess
The physician Borzuy translates the work from Sanskrit into Pahlavi, the Middle Persian language
Ibn al-Muqaffa translates the work into Arabic as Kalīla wa Dimna
Rabbi Joel makes a Hebrew version, the source of most European versions
John of Capua's Latin Directorium Humanae Vitae is printed
Sir Thomas North publishes the first English translation, The Morall Philosophie of Doni
Franklin Edgerton publishes his reconstruction of the original Sanskrit text
Patrick Olivelle's translation, based on Edgerton's reconstruction, is published by Oxford University Press

sections.origins:
The Panchatantra (Sanskrit for 'Five Treatises') is an ancient Indian collection of interrelated animal fables in Sanskrit verse and prose, set within a frame story. Its prelude names an octogenarian Brahmin, Vishnusharma, as its author, teaching the principles of good government to three princes of Amarasakti, the king of Mahilaropya. Some South Indian recensions and Southeast Asian versions name Vasubhaga instead. Most scholars agree that Vishnusharma is a fictitious name, and Patrick Olivelle says it is unclear whether he was a real person at all. Olivelle and others hold that the author was probably a Hindu, and not a Buddhist or Jain, though probably not a devotee of Vishnu, since the text neither speaks against Shiva, Indra and other deities nor avoids invoking them with reverence.

Various places of composition have been proposed, among them Kashmir, south-western India and South India, and the question has been controversial. The text quotes verses identical to some in the Arthasastra, and it draws on the Dharma and Artha shastras and on folk and literary storytelling. Legends with anthropomorphic animals appear in texts from the early centuries of the 1st millennium BCE, such as chapter 4.1 of the Chandogya Upanishad. It shares many stories with the Buddhist Jataka tales, and Olivelle writes that it is uncertain whether its author borrowed from the Jatakas or the Mahabharata, or drew on a common treasury of oral and literary tales.
sections.content:
The Panchatantra is a series of interwoven fables, many of which give animals human virtues and vices. Apart from a short introduction it has five parts, each with a main frame story that contains embedded stories, often with further stories inside them, and the characters also quote epigrammatic verses to make a point. For the benefit of three ignorant princes, it illustrates nīti, roughly prudent worldly conduct or 'the wise conduct of life'. Book 1, Mitra-bheda, the longest at about 45% of the work, follows the jackal Damanaka, an unemployed minister in a lion's kingdom, and his moralising companion Karataka, who conspire to break up the lion king's friendships. Book 2, Mitra-samprapti, about 22%, follows a crow, a mouse, a turtle and a deer, and stresses the value of friendship and teamwork.

Book 3, Kakolukiyam, about 26%, is about war and peace: weaker crows, creatures of the day, defeat the stronger owls by wit, since the crow king heeds his counsellor Ciramjivin and the owl king ignores Raktaksa. Books 4 and 5 together make up about 7%. Book 4, Labdhapranasam, gives negative examples of what to avoid, such as yielding to peer pressure or to soothing words with cunning behind them. Book 5, Aparikshitakarakam, warns against hasty action, with lessons such as getting the facts and not building castles in the air; almost all its characters are human.
sections.making:
The text's date is uncertain. It was translated into Pahlavi around 550 CE, which gives the latest limit of its existence. The earliest limit is unclear. According to Olivelle, the current scholarly consensus places it around 300 CE, though he reminds readers that this is only an educated guess. Johannes Hertel dated it to around 200 BCE, holding that individual fables were already ancient by then. Gillian Adams writes that it may be a product of the Vedic period but that its age cannot be ascertained with confidence, because the original Sanskrit version has been lost. It is also said to have approximated its current literary form within the 4th to 6th centuries CE, and no Sanskrit text from before 1000 CE has survived.

Old manuscripts carry varying titles, among them Tantrakhyayika, Panchakhyanaka, Panchakhyana and Tantropakhyana. Hertel found several Indian recensions, among them the oldest available Sanskrit one, the Tantrakhyayika of Kashmir, and the North Western Family text by the Jain monk Purnabhadra of 1199 CE, which blends and rearranges at least three earlier versions. Edgerton studied all the texts that seemed to go back to the lost Sanskrit original and believed he had reconstructed it, a version known as the Southern Family text. The animal names in the Sanskrit are creative, with double meanings that point both to the animal and to a human personality.
sections.reception:
In the Indian tradition the Panchatantra is a nitishastra, a treatise on political science and human conduct. Early Western scholars read it in different ways. Hertel thought it had a Machiavellian character, and Edgerton wrote that its so-called morals have no bearing on morality, being unmoral and often immoral, since they glorify shrewdness and practical wisdom in the affairs of life, especially of government. Other scholars dismiss this view as one-sided and read the stories as teaching dharma, or proper moral conduct. Olivelle says that the debate, whether the text supports unscrupulous Machiavellian politics or demands ethical conduct from those holding high office, shows the text's rich ambiguity. Konrad Meisig holds that it has been wrongly presented as a textbook for educating princes in the rules of the Arthasastra, and that it is instead a book for the 'Little Man' to develop niti, and a work of social satire.

Niklas Bengtsson calls it certainly the first work ever written down for children, whose influence on fables, fairy tales and children's literature has therefore been enormous. The French fabulist Jean de La Fontaine acknowledged in his Second Fables that the greatest part was inspired by Pilpay, an Indian sage. Doris Lessing noted that until comparatively recently anyone with a literary education in the West knew the Fables of Bidpai as a great Eastern classic.
sections.survival:
The work reached Persia in the Sassanid reign of Anoushiravan, when his physician Borzuy translated it from Sanskrit into Pahlavi, around 550 CE; one dating gives 570 CE. According to the story in Ferdowsi's Shah Nama, Borzuy had gone to India in search of a herb that revives the dead and was told that the herb is the scientist and the book the way to knowledge. Hans Bakker places his visit at the kingdom of Kannauj in the 6th century. His Pahlavi version is now lost. It was translated into Syriac and then, around 750 CE, into Arabic by Ibn al-Muqaffa as Kalila wa Dimna, in which the jackals' names became the name of the whole work. Ibn al-Muqaffa added a chapter on the trial of Dimna, and the political theorist Jennifer London suggests that he used the fables to express risky political views in a metaphorical way.

Almost all pre-modern European translations come from the Arabic. A Greek version by Simeon Seth followed in 1080, a Spanish one in 1252 and a Hebrew one by Rabbi Joel in the 12th century. John of Capua put the Hebrew into Latin as Directorium Humanae Vitae, printed in 1480, the source of most European versions. Anton Francesco Doni made an Italian version in 1552, from which Sir Thomas North made the first English translation in 1570. Buddhist monks carried the text north to Tibet and China and east to Southeast Asia, and Persian prose versions of the 12th and 15th centuries led to a Turkish one.
sections.legacy:
It is called certainly the most frequently translated literary product of India. There is a version in nearly every major language of India and, according to Olivelle, 200 versions in more than 50 languages elsewhere; an older estimate by Jacob gave 112 versions in at least 38 languages. In Indonesia it is Tantri Kamandaka, with 360 fables; in Laos it is Nandaka-prakarana and in Thailand Nang Tantrai. Its stories are also the source of several in the Arabian Nights, and of many Western nursery rhymes and ballads. Folk tale motifs in Boccaccio, La Fontaine and the Brothers Grimm have been linked to it.

Some stories resemble Aesop's Fables: The Ass in the Panther's Skin, The Broken Pot beside The Milkmaid and Her Pail, and The Gold-Giving Snake beside The Man and the Serpent. Max Muller held that animal fables had their principal source in India, but this single-origin hypothesis is now generally discarded in favour of the view that fable motifs arose independently in many cultures, and the relation to Mesopotamian and Greek fables is hotly debated. In modern times Theodor Benfey used it as the basis of comparative literature. Arthur Ryder's translation of 1925 remains popular, and in the 1990s Chandra Rajan's Penguin version and Patrick Olivelle's Oxford version of 1997 appeared.

summary: The Panchatantra is an ancient Indian collection of animal fables in Sanskrit, in five treatises, by an unknown author, probably composed around 300 CE. Carried through Pahlavi, Arabic and Hebrew, it reached Europe and Southeast Asia and has been called the most frequently translated literary product of India.
